I like many of you am here because of the rampant censorship on reddit. I also like many of you were part of reddit from its early days when it was RAW and it was great. And I think over time I've realized that there are some fundamental issues with voting systems that inherently CREATE censorship, in which the only way you can solve is by then censoring those that are trying to censor. Let me explain that.

So the reddit issue IMO is one part reddit, one part users. The issue with users is moot. If you have a site like reddit the users vote and that's that. If the userbase is too young and inexperienced to understand your viewpoint, it doesn't matter, it's a user run site. That in itself isn't really censorship, but a lot of times the users are seeking to censor your post by making it disappear. I think most of us are in agreement that this is okay for the most part.

The second part is the active and rampant amount of moderation, and that shit came on like a hurricane. Within the last 6 months or so it just slammed the site in almost every subreddit. The leaks all but confirm this is top down. I think it's obvious to see this is a site struggling to clean up it's image to court advertisers. I even made a post about this yesterday that was ghosted (what a fucking surprise!)

That being said, back to point one. This is where things become problematic. In my opinion, and I'm a nobody, but as far as nobodies go, I've been posting since the BBS days. I'm a member of an uncountable number of websites, forums etc by this point. I've got probably way more posts under my belt than I want to admit, I don't want to know how much of my life I've lost to the internet really.

What I've learned is that the absolute strongest method to enforce free speech is to allow users control in content they PARTICIPATE in and CREATE. But not give users the ability to create a PREFERENCE to content. The way that most forums work on is in a bump system (last post to the top), or alternatively in a sort of date created. The bump sort has a unique element to it. It promotes exciting and controversial topics. And within those topics, the replies are all linear (though they can reply to other posts in the thread and reference them in quotes).

No ones posts "disappear" without direct moderate involvement. This encourages rampant participation and forces the user to pick threads they want to reply in, not be spoon fed "what they probably want to see." It encourages a closer connection to the website and has a more balanced way of dispensing content.

I think changing the sort to "last submitted" and focusing moderator effort on combining duplicate threads would position this website in a way that would be advantageous. "The other reddit" is a nice way to start things here and get things seeded. But look forward. This should be a website where the outcasts of the internet can collect and post the steaks that the children can't eat. Where no one gets to say "I don't want to see that" or "no one should be able to see that."

Something to think about!

I earned my license when I was 22 and have been in the industry for a little over 2 years now. I'm here to answer any questions you may have about the industry, the position, investing, finance, etc. Ask away!
I am a 23 year old licensed securities representative (or stockbroker as it's more commonly known.) Ask me anything.
Personally, I'm curious about your journey to becoming a securities representative... does that require a degree or just some form of certification? Was it an expensive process?

Generally, it requires a degree or relevant work experience. But you really only have to pass the Series 7 and 63 licensing exams. I have experience in banking and the bank where I work actually offered the position to me after a lengthy 3 hour interview. I was extremely lucky as most people my age are never selected.

The cost was not my responsibility but I have heard from our control officers that it cost around $20k for everything (time off work for studying, materials, website access, question database, classes, etc.) The test itself is fairly cheap to register for but you must be sponsored by a broker-dealer.

For someone that isn't that familiar with stocks, there seems to be a rather steep learning curve. What are the most important things you look for to determine how a stock is performing? Why are penny stocks a joke, is it simply because they are too fresh and haven't proved themselves by meeting a higher level?

There's quite a few things. Firstly, you can compare it to other stocks within the same sector/field. In my opinion, the second most important variable to research are the ratios. For example, there's a neat one called the current ratio.

Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities

Just as an example, we can use iRobot. Based off the data for 12/2014, we get a ratio of 3.78:1. What this means is that for every dollar the company owes, they have $3.78 to pay it back.

Lots of penny stock companies are fronts for the mob, the market is prone to manipulation easily (like wolf of wall st.) And they are just not a safe thing to play with.
What is a typical career path for the average stockbroker? What are your career aspirations in the field?

Honestly, how do you feel about what you do? I've thought about finance but I've always viewed it as selling my soul in a certain sense. Have you thought about it like that or is it just a good career where you can earn solid money?

I don't want to sound like I'm coming off as offended but I'm curious why you would think finance is selling your soul? There's always bad people in an industry who only look out for themselves or cheat people, but I help people make the right investment decisions based on their objectives and risk tolerance. I help make sure the right people get their money when they pass away, I do the research for them in break it down in a simple to understand manner. I'm compensated for my knowledge in the industry. I help people, I don't harm people.

If you do a good job, you can earn lots of money. I know a few people making a little over six figures and they've only been brokers for 2-3 years.

Truthfully? Because the last thing somebody should do to invest money is pay a commission off the top of it. Very few brokers know how to beat the market, and the ones who can are in extremely high demand. When I interviewed for an investment banking job and told them my personal strategy (index funds combined with fixed income if I had the money for such a thing) they laughed and asked how the fuck I could make that sound sexy, and why a potential customer would use me when they could just do that themselves. It's a great question, but that doesn't stop it from being the most sound strategy for most people. I can't in good conscience sell the merits of some rockstar fund manager so the client can pay 10x the fees of an index fund just to not beat the market because the majority don't, and the majority of the ones that do can't do so consistently. The truth is most brokers are just glorified salesman, and most people would just invest in the least risky, lowest fee way possible if the were properly informed. The problem is, brokers aren't there to properly inform people, they're there to get clients, and the fact that those things are different is most of the problem.

How much do you make?

Do you feel that people treat you differently because you're young?

Yes! A lot of older clients tend to ask me a few more questions as if they're gauging my knowledge in a certain subject and I've noticed the younger clients don't. This could just be based on the fact that our older clients have more experience or it could be the fact that I'm extremely young.

Right now, I'm making $120k.

Drop-in electronic fire control for Ruger 10/22

"Bulzi" has manufactured a VERY nice electronic trigger for the 10/22, designed to use as many off the shelf parts as possible. It runs off a nine volt battery, and here is a video of it being demonstrated.

I've communicated with Bulzi recently, and he still has some trigger systems left for sale: they're 500 US apiece! Steep for a trigger, but pretty cheap for an e-trigger (they're usually about three grand, and only used on Olympic Match firearms).

Electronic triggers are appealing because 1) they are fully adjustable, with no smithing required 2) they potentially solve the bullpup trigger problem 3) they normalize reliance on electronic control systems, which opens up a world of previously unthinkable accessories, like servo-actuated firing action.
